data.content_ref: inline:The target's central mechanism commits a conflation fallacy. Popper explicitly argued that preferring a well-tested theory for action is justified by the current state of critical discussion — the theory presently best withstands criticism — without any commitment to the future resembling the past. This is a synchronic, non-inductive evaluation: 'B is currently the least-criticized available option.' The target equates ALL uses of 'should be used' with a diachronic inductive prediction ('B will continue to survive'), but a Popperian can consistently say 'use B now because it is currently the best survivor of criticism' while remaining agnostic about whether B will survive tomorrow. Since the target's entire derivation of 'necessarily smuggles in induction' rests on this conflation, and since Popper's actual framework provides a non-inductive route to preference, the target's claim that radical skepticism is the 'only consistent Popperian stance' is false. Furthermore, the mechanism's concluding sentence — 'It follows that the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all' — is a non sequitur: even if induction were smuggled, that would not imply that the structure of the theory (testability, explanatory power, severity of tests) was irrelevant to outcomes; it would only mean the justification for preference relies on an additional premise.
